                                                             ro
study ES were calculated using hedge’s g. For all significant ES, factors such as age, fitness, and relative

                                                       -p
intensity of the exercise intervention were entered separately as moderators to determine whether these

                                                 re
factors may have influenced the thermoregulatory response to exercise. Significance was set a priori at

p<0.05.


   2. Results
                                         lP
                                  na
    Of the 1,222 potentially studies that emerged from our search , 10 qualified (Figure 1) [14–21,32,33].

Five studies had multiple exercise intensity intervention arms, which yielded 18 interventions
                            ur
[15,18,21,32]. Descriptive characteristics and thermoregulatory outcomes are presented in Table 1. There

                     Jo
was a total of 211 participants (mean= 19  6 participants per study, range= 5-34 participants per study)

who were mostly male (70%), unacclimatized to the heat, and physically inactive (70%). Six of the

studies included adults (mean age: 25 1 years) and four included pubescent (n=2) or prepubescent (n=2)

children (mean age:12  2 years). The overall % body fat (BF%) for the Hi-BF group (n=107) was 36.7 

11.8% (range: 22-68.8%) and 17.69  5.74% (range: 10.8-26.3%) for the Lo-BF group (n= 104), with a

difference between the groups of 19.01 8.8% (p<0.001). VO2max was 50.42  9.3 ml kg-1 min-1 which

was poor to excellent for men of this age and good to superior for women[34].




                                                                                                            7
                                          Journal Pre-proof

    Of the 18 interventions, approximately 16% used absolute metabolic heat production (k=3), 6%

absolute workload (k=1), 38% metabolic heat production relative to total body mass (k=7), 6% fixed

metabolic heat production relative to lean body mass (k=1), 6% fixed metabolic heat production relative

to body surface area (k=1), and 28% used relative VO2max or VO2peak (k=5) as the measure of exercise

intensity (Figure 2). Post exercise Tcore reported in the included studies did not exceed 38°C (37.72 

0.38C). Environmental temperature and humidity ranged from 25-40.3°C and 26-50%, respectively. All

exercise protocols were between 30-60 minutes with an overall relative exercise intensity between 44.1

and 71.4% VO2max.                                                  of
    Using the Downs and Black checklist assessment tool, we found that eight studies exhibited moderate
                                                             ro
methodological quality[14–19,21,32] and two studies exhibited low methodological quality [20,33]

                                                      -p
(Supplemental Table 2). Methodological quality ranged from 45-61% of the items satisfied. None of the

                                                re
10 studies were characterized as randomized controlled trials.

   RVE revealed no differences in Tcore (ES=0.21, 95% C.I. -0.53-0.96, p=0.370), Tsk, (ES=0.799,
                                        lP
95% C.I. -3.06-4.66, p=0.231), or WBSL (ES=0.28, C.I. -1.093-1.67, p=0.46) between groups in response


                                 na
to an aerobic exercise intervention in the heat. Only 7 out of 18 interventions normalized metabolic heat

production to total body mass and only 5 out of 18 interventions normalized exercise intensity to external

workload.                  ur
   3. Discussion
                    Jo
The evidence surrounding the effect of body fat on thermoregulation during exercise in the heat is limited;

the purpose of this systematic review and meta-analyses was to overcome this limitation and characterize

factors that may influence the relationship between body fat and thermoregulatory outcomes during

exercise in the heat in a healthy population. Overall, the included studies were heterogeneous. We must

recognize the study designs or subject characteristics in the current literature confound our understanding

of the independent influence of body fat on thermoregulatory outcomes. Understanding these factors not

only benefits the development of future studies, but it also sheds light on the whether or not body fat can




                                                                                                              8
                                          Journal Pre-proof

independently predict thermoregulatory outcomes and continue to be characterized as a risk factor for

impaired thermoregulation in the heat. Interestingly, RVE revealed that there were no differences in

 Tcore, Tsk, and WBSL between Hi-BF and Lo-BF groups in interventions that performed unbias

comparisons between Hi-BF and Lo-BF groups.

        Prescribed exercise intensities between interventions of included studies were extremely diverse

(Figure 2), which could have contributed to the inter-study and potentially inter-individual variability of

thermoregulatory outcomes between groups. Higher variability among data reduces the ability to detect

                                                                   of
statistical significance [35]. Traditionally, researchers in environmental physiology prescribed exercise

based on the participant’s relative VO2max to perform unbias comparisons between groups [36–38]. This
                                                             ro
method was implemented to reduce bias between participants of different fitness levels[36]. Although this

                                                       -p
method may provide valuable information in settings that require self-paced work[12], the approach is


                                                 re
worrisome as it often results in differences in requirements for heat loss [36]. Jay & Cramer (2015)

proposed an optimal between group study design to control for factors that modulate thermoregulatory
                                         lP
responses during exercise in the heat by utilizing metabolic heat production. Fixing metabolic heat


                                 na
production among participants suggests that each participant is experiencing the same thermal stimulus

and differences in heat loss can be attributed to the independent factor of interest [36]. Although 12 of the

                           ur
18 interventions in this systematic review prescribed exercise intensity based on metabolic heat


                    Jo
production [14–16,32], only 7 accounted for differences in total body mass (i.e. W/kg). If total body mass

is not corrected (when prescribing exercise based on metabolic heat production), Larger individuals

working at the same metabolic rate as lighter people have a greater “heat sink” and therefore, requires

more energy to raise their Tcore [12]. This mechanism is considered protective and often associated with

a lower vulnerability to heat illness in larger individuals [12]. This further complicates the independent

influence of body fat on thermoregulation as individuals with high body fat tend to be higher in body

mass [12]. Moreover, individuals with high body fat tend to also have lower surface area to mass ratios,

which translates to less surface area available for evaporation of sweat from the skin per unit body mass.

In summary, it is difficult to ascertain whether differences in thermoregulatory response between Hi-BF


                                                                                                              9
                                           Journal Pre-proof

and Lo-BF are attributed to body fat when body surface area and body mass are also different between

groups. Interestingly, the meta-analysis performed in the current study resulted in unclear ESs and non-

significant findings. It is important to note that the number of interventions included were small, which

makes it difficult to determine whether the findings were a lack of association or the result of type II

error.

         Dervis et al.a is arguably the most internally valid study to examine the effect of body fat on

thermoregulation during exercise in the heat and should be modeled to examine the influence of


                                                                    of
independent factors on thermoregulation in the heat. This investigation matched their Hi-BF and Lo-BF

groups in pairs for both total body mass and body surface area. Participants cycled for 60 min at 550W.
                                                              ro
To independently examine body fat, groups only differed in body fat percentage (difference of 21%

                                                       -p
between groups). Interestingly, they found that Tcore was significantly higher in the Hi-BF group


                                                 re
compared to Lo-BF, with no differences in WBSL or Tsk. Dervis et al. (2015) reported that differences in

 Tcore with no corresponding thermoeffector response suggests differences in either physiological
                                         lP
control (i.e. thermosensitivity or prolonged onset threshold) or conductivity of body tissues (i.e. low


                                  na
conductivity of fat tissue). By eliminating the confounding effects of total body mass, metabolic heat

production, and body surface area through study design, there is stronger evidence to suggest that body fat

                            ur
may independently influence thermoregulatory responses. It is imperative that future work assessing the


                    Jo
effect of body fat on thermoregulation during exercise in the heat control for these confounding variables

in their study design. This will allow for a more comprehensive and precise evaluation of the true

influence of adiposity as the result of a single study does not provide enough information to establish the

state of existing knowledge.

         The included studies present several other factors that may influence the relationship between

body fat and thermoregulatory responses to exercise in heat. Dougherty et al. (2009) examined differences

in thermoregulatory responses between obese and lean boys before and after they were heat acclimatized.

Interestingly, Difference in Tcore between Day 6 (heat acclimatized) and Day 1(heat unacclimatized)

was -0.23°C. and -0.05°C for lean and obese, respectively. In other words, although both lean and obese


                                                                                                            10
                                           Journal Pre-proof

groups experienced the physiological adaptations necessary to incur heat acclimatization, the obese boys

acclimatized at a slower rate compared to the lean boys[21]. The participants in Dervis et al. (2016) were

assumed to be unacclimatized to heat, but researchers were uncertain whether or not there were

differences in heat acclimatization status between groups. Differences in heat acclimatization status can

greatly affect thermoregulation and should be strongly considered in future investigations examining

thermoregulatory responses to heat in Hi-BF vs. Lo-BF. Future investigations must also consider post-

exercise Tcore. All Tcore data from included studies suggested that participants’ Tcores did not exceed


                                                                     of
38°C, which is below the threshold for exercise-induced hyperthermia(<38.5°C). Thermoeffector

responses are considered a function of changes in body temperature and body temperature changes are
                                                              ro
heavily weighted by the influence of Tcore (opposed to Tsk)[40,41]. Therefore, as Tcore stayed below

                                                        -p
<38.5°C (i.e. hyperthermic zone) it is difficult to acertain whether differences in thermoeffector output


                                                  re
would have occurred between Hi-BF and Lo-BF groups at higher Tcores. Lastly, the majority of the

included investigations assessed steady state exercise. Eliciting steady state exercise may have diminished

                                          lP
the influence of BF% on Tcore and WBSL, leading to no differences between groups [42].


                                  na
        Despite the many strengths of this systematic review and meta-analyses, there are limitations that

must be addressed. First, the included studies only reflect children and adults under the age of 30. Future

                            ur
investigations should examine older adults as this aging is associated with differences in degree of


                    Jo
adiposity and adipose tissue function as well as an enhanced risk of thermoregulatory dysfunction[43–45].

It should also be noted that although prepubertal children differ from adults in morphology and other

physical factors, there does not appear to be maturational differences that influence children’s ability to

thermoregulate in the heat, compared to adults [46]. Additionally, the body fat groups were characterized

by the authors of each individual study. Therefore, there was some overlap in BF% characterization

between studies. Lastly, although a meta-analysis of studies controlling for metabolic heat production and

body mass were performed, they were substantially underpowered. Aforementioned, underpowered

analyses make it difficult to conclude whether the findings were the result of a lack of association or the

result of type II error. As the literature currently stands, there are limited randomized controlled trials that


                                                                                                              11
                                           Journal Pre-proof

utilize the appropriate study designs to examine the independent influence of body fat on

thermoregulation in the heat. To accurately examine the independent influence of body fat, randomized

controlled trials using experimental approaches controlling for confounders of thermoregulatory response

during exercise in the heat are warranted.



Conclusion

The included studies were heterogeneous and many did not control for confounding factors that affect


                                                                   of
thermoregulation in the heat such as metabolic heat production, body mass, body surface area, and heat

acclimatization. Studies performing unbiased comparisons between Hi-BF and Lo-BF groups are
                                                                ro
recommended to further characterize the adverse effects of obesity on thermoregulation in the heat

                                                       -p
[15,36,38]. Future investigations should also examine differences in Hi-BF and Lo-BF groups who were


                                                 re
hyperthermic. It is possible that differences in thermoeffector responses between groups are a function of

changes in thermoeffector onset threshold or thermosensitivity, that may only be present after higher

Tcores.                                   lP
Practical Implications
                                   na
                            ur
          There are current methodological concerns in research studies surrounding the influence of body



    
                     Jo
          fat on thermoregulation during exercise in the heat

          Future investigations need to make unbiased comparisons (i.e. control for confounding factors

          such as metabolic heat production, body mass, heat acclimatization, body surface area, etc.)

          between Hi-BF and Lo-BF to examine the independent influence of body fat on thermoregulation

          during exercise in the heat.

18	Abstract
19	Background Daytime napping is used by athletes as a strategy to supplement night time sleep and aid physical performance.
20	However, no meta-analytical overview regarding the impact of napping following a night of normal sleep (7–9 h) on physical
21	performance is available.
22	Objective The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of daytime napping following normal night-time sleep on physical
23	performance in physically active individuals and athletes.
24	Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for
25	Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. Seven electronic databases (i.e., PubMed, Web of Science,
26	Scopus, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, SCIELO, and EBSCOhost) were used to search for relevant studies that investigated the
27	impact of daytime napping, following normal night-time sleep, on physical performance in physically active individuals
28	and athletes, published in any language, and available before September 01, 2022. Studies that included assessments of
29	any physical performance measures were included. QualSyst was used to assess the methodological quality of the studies.
30	Results Of 18 selected articles, 15 were of strong quality and 3 were of moderate quality. Compared with no-nap conditions,
31	physically active individuals and athletes who napped experienced an increase in highest distance (effect size [ES] 1.026;
32	p < 0.001) and total distance (ES 0.737; p < 0.001), and a decrease in fatigue index (ES 0.839, p = 0.008) during the 5-m
33	shuttle run test (5MSRT). However, napping yielded no effect on muscle force (ES 0.175; p = 0.267). No effect of napping
34	was found in one study that measured sprint performance and in two studies that measured performance during the 30-s
35	Wingate test. Two of three studies reported an increase in jump performance after napping. Two of three studies reported an
36	increase in repeated sprints after napping. One study reported an increase in upper-body power performance after napping,
37	and napping was beneficial for endurance performance in one of two studies.
38	Conclusion Following normal sleep, napping is beneficial for the performance of the 5MSRT, with no significant effect on muscle
39	force. No firm conclusions can be drawn regarding other physical performance measures due to the limited number of studies.

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



The Impact of Daytime Napping Following Normal Night‑Time
Sleep on Physical Performance: A Systematic Review, Meta‑analysis
and Meta‑regression
Omar Boukhris1,9 · Khaled Trabelsi1,2,3 · Haresh Suppiah1,9 · Achraf Ammar4 · Cain C. T. Clark5 · Haitham Jahrami6,7 ·
Hamdi Chtourou1,2,8 · Matthew Driller1,9

Accepted: 20 August 2023
© The Author(s) 2023


Abstract
Background Daytime napping is used by athletes as a strategy to supplement night time sleep and aid physical performance.
However, no meta-analytical overview regarding the impact of napping following a night of normal sleep (7–9 h) on physical
performance is available.
Objective The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of daytime napping following normal night-time sleep on physical
performance in physically active individuals and athletes.
Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for
Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. Seven electronic databases (i.e., PubMed, Web of Science,
Scopus, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL, SCIELO, and EBSCOhost) were used to search for relevant studies that investigated the
impact of daytime napping, following normal night-time sleep, on physical performance in physically active individuals
and athletes, published in any language, and available before September 01, 2022. Studies that included assessments of
any physical performance measures were included. QualSyst was used to assess the methodological quality of the studies.
Results Of 18 selected articles, 15 were of strong quality and 3 were of moderate quality. Compared with no-nap conditions,
physically active individuals and athletes who napped experienced an increase in highest distance (effect size [ES] 1.026;
p < 0.001) and total distance (ES 0.737; p < 0.001), and a decrease in fatigue index (ES 0.839, p = 0.008) during the 5-m
shuttle run test (5MSRT). However, napping yielded no effect on muscle force (ES 0.175; p = 0.267). No effect of napping
was found in one study that measured sprint performance and in two studies that measured performance during the 30-s
Wingate test. Two of three studies reported an increase in jump performance after napping. Two of three studies reported an
increase in repeated sprints after napping. One study reported an increase in upper-body power performance after napping,
and napping was beneficial for endurance performance in one of two studies.
Conclusion Following normal sleep, napping is beneficial for the performance of the 5MSRT, with no significant effect on muscle
force. No firm conclusions can be drawn regarding other physical performance measures due to the limited number of studies.

221	        Hamstring strain injuries (HSIs) remain the most common cause of time lost from

226	
227	likely elevates the risk of a HSI occurring, due to the biomechanical demands placed on the
228	
229	hamstrings (4). Rather than stopping athletes from sprinting, researchers and practitioners

Purpose: Investigate impact of an isometric (ISO) or Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE)

sprinting performance in Australian Footballers. Methods: Twenty-five male athletes

undertook NHE (n = 13) or ISO (n = 12) training across a 38-week period (including pre-

season and in-season). Biceps femoris long head (BFlh) architecture, isometric and eccentric

knee flexor strength were assessed at baseline, end of pre-season (14-weeks) and at the

BFlh fascicle length, thickness, and eccentric strength in Australian Footballers. NHE

 INTRODUCTION

        Hamstring strain injuries (HSIs) remain the most common cause of time lost from

competition in field-based team sports (1), such as Australian Rules Football (ARF) (2).

Athletes are required to perform regular sprinting efforts during ARF competition (3), which

likely elevates the risk of a HSI occurring, due to the biomechanical demands placed on the

hamstrings (4). Rather than stopping athletes from sprinting, researchers and practitioners

                                                                                  D
aim to identify interventions that address modifiable variables associated with HSI risk, such




                            EP
as hamstring muscle architecture and strength (5-8). It is important to consider the impact that

these interventions have on sprint acceleration performance, given this is a key requirement

of ARF and many other field-based team sports.




                              TE
        Including the Nordic hamstring exercise (NHE) as part of a training program reduces

HSI risk in athletes (9, 10). This risk reductive effect may be driven by increases in biceps

femoris long head (BFlh) fascicle length and eccentric knee flexor strength noted after NHE


             C

A

 C

fear of muscle soreness caused by this relatively high-intensity eccentric stimulus (16), which

has led to interest in isometric hamstring exercises interventions.




        Despite interest in isometric hamstring exercises, there has been limited research into

the potential benefits of these interventions on HSI risk factors and sprint performance. One

study found that an isometric hip extension exercise leads to greater improvements in the

76	                           optimizing the sleep environment can be compromised through factors outside of an ath-
77	                           lete’s control [19,20] Athletes face many barriers to sleep, including intensive training and
78	                           competition scheduling, travelling across time zones, and pre-competition anxiety [20].
79	                           Additionally, strict anti-doping and medication policies may limit an elite athlete’s ability
80	                           to trial effective sleep aids such as melatonin [19]. With common sleep-promoting recom-
81	                           mendations having little translation to the unique athlete environment, athletes and their
82	                           coaches need to explore alternatives.
83	                                  Recent reviews link diet to sleep quality and duration [21–25], expanding the essential
84	                           role that nutrition plays in sports performance and recovery. Common dietary themes asso-
85	                           ciated with improved sleep in non-athletes include meal timing, macronutrient composition,
86	                           and dietary supplementation [21–25]. For instance, meal timing and nutritional composition
87	                           are primary cues for peripheral molecular clocks including those in the liver and gut [26,27].
88	                           Alterations of these peripheral clocks through changes in meal timing and composition may
89	                           induce circadian phase shifts, which can result in circadian misalignment [26,28,29]. With
90	                           sleep coinciding with decreases in core body temperature [30,31], eating close to bedtime
91	                           can theoretically impair sleep through metabolic disturbances associated with digestion.
92	                           Further, meal composition can influence the secretion of sleep-regulating hormones such
93	                           as melatonin [28,32]. Melatonin is primarily involved in conveying light/dark signals to
94	                           body physiology, playing a major role in the regulation of the sleep/wake cycle [33]. Data
95	                           suggests that protein and carbohydrate intake likely influence melatonin synthesis indi-
96	                           rectly through the tryptophan (TRP) to large neutral amino acid (LNAA) ratio [28,32,34].
97	                           Tryptophan is an amino acid that shares the same transport system as other LNAAs to
98	                           cross the blood–brain-barrier [32]; therefore, the ratio of TRP:LNAAs within blood plasma
99	                           affects tryptophan availability to the brain and resultant melatonin production [28,32,34].
100	                           Increases in the TRP:LNAA ratio may promote TRP availability, melatonin synthesis, and
101	                           ultimately sleep, which occurs through the intake of carbohydrates or protein sources high
102	                           in TRP and low in other LNAAs (e.g., dairy) [34–36]. Alternatively, an intake of protein
103	                           sources high in LNAA and low in TRP reduces the TRP:LNAA ratio and may hinder
104	                           sleep [34,37,38], but this has not been tested extensively in athletes.
105	                                  Nutritional recommendations for optimizing athlete sleep primarily draw upon lit-
106	                           erature from the general population [13,16,39]. This may not be appropriate for athletes,
107	                           however, with a recent review finding macronutrient intake may influence the sleep quality
108	                           of athletic and non-athletic populations differently [39]. Consumption of high glycaemic
109	                           index (GI) carbohydrates with an evening meal resulted in more disrupted sleep within
110	                           state-level basketballers [40], but resulted in shortened sleep latency within a general popu-
111	                           lation [39,41]. Similarly, a high tryptophan protein supplement consumed in the evening
112	                           improved multiple aspects of sleep quality in healthy males [42], yet had no impact on the
113	                           sleep of well-trained male cyclists [43]. Though the full extent of athlete literature within
114	                           this area is still to be established, it may be speculated that differences in macronutrient
115	                           intake [37,44], nutritional requirements [45], physiological adaptation [46], sleeping be-
116	                           haviours [47,48], and stressors including exercise and competition [20] may have led to
117	                           discrepancies between the nutrition–sleep relationships demonstrated for non-athletic and
118	                           athletic populations.
119	                                  With growing interest in the nutrition–sleep relationship of athletic populations [16,39],
120	                           it is important that nutritional recommendations are guided by data within athletic popula-
121	                           tions, as athlete-specific differences may add confounding factors to the nutrition–sleep
122	                           relationship. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review was to evaluate the evidence for
123	                           the impact of specific dietary factors including composition, timing, and dietary supplement
124	                           use on sleep duration and quality within athletically trained populations.

131	                               This review follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-

136	                               Four electronic databases (CINAHL Complete, Embase, MEDLINE Complete, and

144	                                Included studies met the following criteria: (1) participants were stated as being
145	                           athletes (e.g., student, sub-elite, elite, and/or professional), competitive sportspeople,
146	                           trained (e.g., endurance-trained, resistance-trained), or could be identified as ‘athletically
147	                           trained’ using previously published criteria (see Section 2.2.1); (2) participants within the
148	                           study were healthy non-injured individuals; (3) the study included a nutrient and/or food
149	                           source as the independent variable; (4) the study reported at least one subjective and/or
150	                           objective outcome measure of sleep or sleepiness; (5) the mean age of participants was
151	                           ≥18 years; (6) the study was an original research study; (7) the study was published in
152	                           English as a full-text article in a peer-reviewed journal.
153	                                Although athletically trained criteria may extend to ‘tactical’ athletes (i.e., law enforce-
154	                           ment, military, and rescue personnel that require physical training to optimize occupational
155	                           performance [49]), these populations were excluded from the review due to difficulties
156	                           determining the training status and requirements of these population groups.

158	                           2.2.1. Trained Population Classification
159	                                 Classification of ‘athletically trained’ subjects complied with guidelines for sports-
160	                           science research [50]. These cycling-based guidelines use ‘trained’ terminology when train-
161	                           ing is completed ≥3 times per week, for ≥5 h per week [50]. Therefore, for this review, these
162	                           guidelines were extrapolated to consider populations as ‘trained’ if exercising ≥3 times per
163	                           week, for ≥5 h per week. As such, studies detailing their participant’s training frequency
164	                           and duration at these amounts were deemed eligible for inclusion.

170	                           was then examined by two reviewers (JB, SR) to determine whether inclusion criteria were
171	                           met. Any discrepancies were discussed to reach consensus.

173	                           designed to record information on the study design, methods, and sample population.
174	                           The spreadsheet of extracted data was then screened for accuracy by another reviewer
175	                           (SR). The following variables were extracted from eligible articles: author (year), study
176	                           design, sample size, participant details (age, sex, sport type, training status), study duration,
177	                           intervention/control methodology, sleep assessment methodology, results, and conclusions.

The Impact of Dietary Factors on the Sleep of Athletically
Trained Populations: A Systematic Review
Jackson Barnard 1, *, Spencer Roberts 1 , Michele Lastella 2 , Brad Aisbett 3 and Dominique Condo 1

                                          1   Centre for Sport Research, Deakin University, Geelong, VIC 3220, Australia
                                          2   Appleton Institute for Behavioural Science, Central Queensland University, Wayville, SA 5034, Australia
                                          3   Institute for Physical Activity and Nutrition (IPAN), School of Exercise and Nutrition Sciences,
                                              Deakin University, Geelong, VIC 3220, Australia
                                          *   Correspondence: jgbarnard@deakin.edu.au


                                          Abstract: Many athletic populations report poor sleep, especially during intensive training and
                                          competition periods. Recently, diet has been shown to significantly affect sleep in general populations;
                                          however, little is known about the effect diet has on the sleep of athletically trained populations.
                                          With sleep critical for optimal recovery and sports performance, this systematic review aimed to
                                          evaluate the evidence demonstrating that dietary factors influence the sleep of athletically trained
                                          populations. Four electronic databases were searched from inception to May 2022, with primary
                                          research articles included if they contained a dietary factor(s), an outcome measure of sleep or
                                          sleepiness, and participants could be identified as ‘athletically trained’. Thirty-five studies were
                                          included, with 21 studies assessed as positive quality, 13 as neutral, and one as negative. Sleep or
                                          sleepiness was measured objectively in 46% of studies (n = 16). The review showed that evening
                                          (≥5 p.m.) caffeine intakes >2 mg·kg−1 body mass decreased sleep duration and sleep efficiency,
                                          and increased sleep latency and wake after sleep onset. Evening consumption of high glycaemic
                                          index carbohydrates and protein high in tryptophan may reduce sleep latency. Although promising,
                                          more research is required before the impact of probiotics, cherry juice, and beetroot juice on the sleep

                           be an effective strategy to acutely improve sleep in athletes [18], recommendations to
                           avoid high-intensity exercise in the evening, maintaining regular sleep/wake times, and
                           optimizing the sleep environment can be compromised through factors outside of an ath-
                           lete’s control [19,20] Athletes face many barriers to sleep, including intensive training and
                           competition scheduling, travelling across time zones, and pre-competition anxiety [20].
                           Additionally, strict anti-doping and medication policies may limit an elite athlete’s ability
                           to trial effective sleep aids such as melatonin [19]. With common sleep-promoting recom-
                           mendations having little translation to the unique athlete environment, athletes and their
                           coaches need to explore alternatives.
                                  Recent reviews link diet to sleep quality and duration [21–25], expanding the essential
                           role that nutrition plays in sports performance and recovery. Common dietary themes asso-
                           ciated with improved sleep in non-athletes include meal timing, macronutrient composition,
                           and dietary supplementation [21–25]. For instance, meal timing and nutritional composition
                           are primary cues for peripheral molecular clocks including those in the liver and gut [26,27].
                           Alterations of these peripheral clocks through changes in meal timing and composition may
                           induce circadian phase shifts, which can result in circadian misalignment [26,28,29]. With
                           sleep coinciding with decreases in core body temperature [30,31], eating close to bedtime
                           can theoretically impair sleep through metabolic disturbances associated with digestion.
                           Further, meal composition can influence the secretion of sleep-regulating hormones such
                           as melatonin [28,32]. Melatonin is primarily involved in conveying light/dark signals to
                           body physiology, playing a major role in the regulation of the sleep/wake cycle [33]. Data
                           suggests that protein and carbohydrate intake likely influence melatonin synthesis indi-
                           rectly through the tryptophan (TRP) to large neutral amino acid (LNAA) ratio [28,32,34].
                           Tryptophan is an amino acid that shares the same transport system as other LNAAs to
                           cross the blood–brain-barrier [32]; therefore, the ratio of TRP:LNAAs within blood plasma
                           affects tryptophan availability to the brain and resultant melatonin production [28,32,34].
                           Increases in the TRP:LNAA ratio may promote TRP availability, melatonin synthesis, and
                           ultimately sleep, which occurs through the intake of carbohydrates or protein sources high
                           in TRP and low in other LNAAs (e.g., dairy) [34–36]. Alternatively, an intake of protein
                           sources high in LNAA and low in TRP reduces the TRP:LNAA ratio and may hinder
                           sleep [34,37,38], but this has not been tested extensively in athletes.
                                  Nutritional recommendations for optimizing athlete sleep primarily draw upon lit-
                           erature from the general population [13,16,39]. This may not be appropriate for athletes,
                           however, with a recent review finding macronutrient intake may influence the sleep quality
                           of athletic and non-athletic populations differently [39]. Consumption of high glycaemic
                           index (GI) carbohydrates with an evening meal resulted in more disrupted sleep within
                           state-level basketballers [40], but resulted in shortened sleep latency within a general popu-
                           lation [39,41]. Similarly, a high tryptophan protein supplement consumed in the evening
                           improved multiple aspects of sleep quality in healthy males [42], yet had no impact on the
                           sleep of well-trained male cyclists [43]. Though the full extent of athlete literature within
                           this area is still to be established, it may be speculated that differences in macronutrient
                           intake [37,44], nutritional requirements [45], physiological adaptation [46], sleeping be-
                           haviours [47,48], and stressors including exercise and competition [20] may have led to
                           discrepancies between the nutrition–sleep relationships demonstrated for non-athletic and
                           athletic populations.
                                  With growing interest in the nutrition–sleep relationship of athletic populations [16,39],
                           it is important that nutritional recommendations are guided by data within athletic popula-
                           tions, as athlete-specific differences may add confounding factors to the nutrition–sleep
                           relationship. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review was to evaluate the evidence for
                           the impact of specific dietary factors including composition, timing, and dietary supplement
                           use on sleep duration and quality within athletically trained populations.
 Nutrients 2022, 14, 3271                                                                                             3 of 25




                           2. Materials and Methods
                               This review follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-
                           Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, with PROSPERO trial registration number CRD42021264200.
                           The PRISMA checklist is reported in Supplementary Table S1.

                           2.1. Search Strategy
                               Four electronic databases (CINAHL Complete, Embase, MEDLINE Complete, and
                           SPORTDiscus with Full Text) were searched from database inception to May 2022. The fol-
                           lowing search terms and strategy were used for all databases: (Athlet* OR Sport* OR Player*
                           OR Exercis* OR Active OR Elite OR Trained OR Compet*) AND (Nutri* OR M?cronutri*
                           OR Food OR Diet OR Diets OR Meal* OR Supplement*) AND (Sleep* OR Nap OR Naps
                           OR Napping)). The search was limited only to human studies available in English.

                           2.2. Eligibility Criteria
                                Included studies met the following criteria: (1) participants were stated as being
                           athletes (e.g., student, sub-elite, elite, and/or professional), competitive sportspeople,
                           trained (e.g., endurance-trained, resistance-trained), or could be identified as ‘athletically
                           trained’ using previously published criteria (see Section 2.2.1); (2) participants within the
                           study were healthy non-injured individuals; (3) the study included a nutrient and/or food
                           source as the independent variable; (4) the study reported at least one subjective and/or
                           objective outcome measure of sleep or sleepiness; (5) the mean age of participants was
                           ≥18 years; (6) the study was an original research study; (7) the study was published in
                           English as a full-text article in a peer-reviewed journal.
                                Although athletically trained criteria may extend to ‘tactical’ athletes (i.e., law enforce-
                           ment, military, and rescue personnel that require physical training to optimize occupational
                           performance [49]), these populations were excluded from the review due to difficulties
                           determining the training status and requirements of these population groups.

                           2.2.1. Trained Population Classification
                                 Classification of ‘athletically trained’ subjects complied with guidelines for sports-
                           science research [50]. These cycling-based guidelines use ‘trained’ terminology when train-
                           ing is completed ≥3 times per week, for ≥5 h per week [50]. Therefore, for this review, these
                           guidelines were extrapolated to consider populations as ‘trained’ if exercising ≥3 times per
                           week, for ≥5 h per week. As such, studies detailing their participant’s training frequency
                           and duration at these amounts were deemed eligible for inclusion.

                           2.3. Study Selection and Data Extraction
                                Articles identified in the systematic search were exported to Covidence software
                           (Melbourne, Australia) following duplicate removal. The title and abstract of each retrieved
                           record were screened by one reviewer (JB). The full text of each relevant screened article
                           was then examined by two reviewers (JB, SR) to determine whether inclusion criteria were
                           met. Any discrepancies were discussed to reach consensus.
                                Data from eligible studies were extracted by one reviewer (JB) into a spreadsheet
                           designed to record information on the study design, methods, and sample population.
                           The spreadsheet of extracted data was then screened for accuracy by another reviewer
                           (SR). The following variables were extracted from eligible articles: author (year), study
                           design, sample size, participant details (age, sex, sport type, training status), study duration,
                           intervention/control methodology, sleep assessment methodology, results, and conclusions.
                           The mean ± SD for sleep outcomes of interest were recorded (see Section 2.3.1). Studies
                           were then categorized into themes according to the dietary factor investigated.

                           2.3.1. Sleep Definitions and Outcomes of Interest
                                This systematic review included studies reporting objective and/or subjective mea-
                           sures of sleep or sleepiness. Table 1 provides the definitions of key sleep-related terms used
                           throughout this review [6].

                           Table 1. Sleep related definitions [6].

                                     Sleep efficiency (SE)            The percentage of time in bed that was spent asleep.
                                  Sleep onset latency (SOL)           The period of time between bedtime and sleep onset.
                                                                        The amount of time spent awake after sleep has

                                Sleep quality is a widely used term with no single definition [51]. Subjective sleep
                           quality is defined in relation to feeling rested and restored upon waking, tiredness dur-
                           ing the day, and number of awakenings at night [52]. Objectively, good sleep quality as
                           determined by the National Sleep Foundation, is defined in relation to sleep onset latency
                           (≤15 min), number of awakenings greater than five minutes (≤1), wake after sleep onset
                           (≤20 min), and sleep efficiency (≥85%) [51].

                           2.4. Quality Assessment
                                 The methodological quality and risk of bias within each study was independently
                           assessed by two reviewers (JB, SR), using the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics Qual-
                           ity Criteria Checklist: Primary Research tool [53]. Discrepancies were discussed between
                           the reviewers, with another author (DC) consulted if a consensus could not be reached.
                           The quality criteria checklist contains ten validity questions relating to: (1) research ques-
                           tions; (2) participant selection; (3) study groups’ comparability; (4) participant withdrawal;
                           (5) study blinding; (6) interventions and comparisons; (7) outcome measures; (8) statistical
                           analysis; (9) conclusions; (10) conflicts of interest. Study quality was classified as positive
                           (+) if question 2, 3, 6, and 7, as well as one other question were scored with a ‘yes’; neutral
                           (ø) if any of the questions 2, 3, 6, and 7 did not receive a ‘yes’; or negative (−) if six or more
                           questions were answered with a ‘no’.

                           3. Results

                           tion searching. There were 2991 duplicates removed, and of the 7220 records remaining,
                           7101 articles were removed based on title and abstract as they did not include trained
                           populations, sleep outcomes, or a dietary factor. After assessing 119 full-text articles for
                           eligibility, 35 articles were included for review. The PRISMA flow chart for the systematic
                           review is presented in Figure 1.

Training intervention




 C      As part of their weekly team resistance training sessions, all participants completed

one of either the NHE or ISO hold exercises. During the training intervention, all participants

also undertook a periodised sprint training intervention (Figure 2) prior to their on-field

football specific sessions. The frequency of both the sprinting and resistance training sessions

during the in-season period depended on the match schedule, with either one or two sessions

undertaken per week, with the sprinting and resistance training interventions matched

between the groups. When two sessions per week (both sprinting and resistance training)




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 were undertaken, these were completed on non-consecutive days of the week (typically a

Tuesday and Thursday with a Saturday match). The training prescription was matched for the

NHE and ISO hold exercises across the entire intervention period and was two sets of four

repetitions (Table 1). Both the NHE and ISO hold exercise were undertaken for four second

repetitions to match total time under tension between the groups.



Nordic hamstring exercise training. A video of the NHE can be found in Supplemental

                                                                                  D
Video 1 (Supplemental Digital Content 1). Participants undertook the NHE with their ankles

secured underneath a fixed piece of gym equipment that allowed a standardised kneeling




                            EP
height and position for all repetitions. This was preferred to the partner held version of the

NHE, where the strength of the partner may limit the effectiveness of the effort. For each




                              TE
repetition, participants only performed the lowering (eccentric) portion of the NHE over a

four second period. After each repetition, participants were instructed to use their arms and

flex their hips to assist themselves in returning to the starting position, avoiding any

concentric contraction of the hamstrings. Once additional weight was utilised, the participants



             C
were required to hold weight plates totalling 5, 7.5 or 10kg over their xiphoid process, per

previous work (REF). All NHE training was preceded by a warm up set of three submaximal,




A
bodyweight repetitions and following each training set participants were afforded a 2 min




 C
rest. For all NHE training sessions across the intervention period, participants completed two

sets of four repetitions, which has previously been shown as an effective dose to maintain

eccentric knee flexor strength and BFlh fascicle lengths in recreational individuals (13).



Isometric hamstring training. A video of the ISO hold can be found in Supplemental Video

2 (Supplemental Digital Content 2). Participants started in a kneeling position, with their

ankles secured under a piece of gym equipment. The position was similar to the typical break




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 point of the NHE, where their hips were slightly flexed, with a forward lean of approximately

45 degrees at the knee and using their arms to brace the upper body on a bench placed in

front of them. With the cues “hips under, quiet bum” participants were instructed to “pull up”

as hard and fast as they can against the fixed gym equipment for four seconds. Prior to each

training session participants undertook a sub-maximal warm up consisting of three ISO hold

repetitions at 50%, 75% and approximately 95% of their perceived maximum. Following

each training effort, participants were afforded a 30 second rest prior to the next attempt, with

                                                                                  D
two minutes rest between sets. For all ISO training sessions across the intervention period,

participants completed two sets of four repetitions, with training time matched between the

NHE and ISO groups.

Periodised sprint training. Prior to all on-field football specific training sessions, participants

undertook a periodised sprint intervention for the entire study period (Supplemental Tables 1a

– 1c, Supplemental Digital Content 3). All sprint training was preceded by an on-field group

warm up, following which participants undertook sub-maximal sprinting efforts prior to any



             C
maximal attempts. For all the maximal efforts, participants were paired together based on

their maximal sprint velocity and undertook their efforts in a race format where they were




A
motivated to run faster than the person next to them. Across the study period, the number and




 C
distance of the sprinting exposures was periodised to provide a progressive stimulus (Figure

2). This periodisation was planned on the assumption that the participants could potentially

not undertake any sprinting efforts during their football specific sessions or matches.

Therefore, should this occur, they will have still been exposed to a sprinting stimulus as part

of this prescription. During all sprint training efforts (≥25km/hr), velocity was collected

utilising GPS data (OptimEye S5, 10Hz, Catapult Sports, Melbourne, Australia) and recorded

as absolute and relative values. Relative velocity was determined as a percentage of each




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 participant’s maximum recorded velocity, which was updated if it increased throughout the

study.



Outcome measures

BFlh architecture. The methods to assess BFlh architecture has been previously reported (5,

22, 23) Briefly, muscle thickness, pennation angle and fascicle length of the BFlh was

determined from ultrasound images taken along the longitudinal axis of the muscle belly

                                                                                 D
utilising a two-dimensional, B-mode ultrasound (frequency, 12Mhz; depth, 8cm; field of

view, 14 x 47mm) (GE Healthcare Vivid-i, Wauwatosa, U.S.A). The scanning site was




                           EP
determined as the halfway point between the ischial tuberosity and the knee joint fold, along

the line of the BFlh. All architectural assessments were performed with the participant prone




                             TE
on a massage plinth, after 5mins of inactivity. The orientation of the probe was then

manipulated by the assessor (RGT) whose reliability has been previously reported (23).



         Once the images were collected, analysis was undertaken off-line (MicroDicom,

Version 0.7.8, Bulgaria). Muscle thickness was defined as the distance between the


            C
superficial and intermediate aponeuroses of the BFlh. Pennation angle was defined as the

angle between the inferior aponeurosis and a fascicle of interest. The aponeurosis angle for



A
both aponeuroses was determined as the angle between the line marked as the aponeurosis



 C
and an intersecting horizontal reference line across the captured image (24, 25). As the entire

fascicle was not visible in the field of view of the probe, its length was estimated via the

following equation (25):




         FL=sin (AA+90°) x MT/sin(180°-(AA+180°-PA)).




   Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 Where FL=fascicle length, AA=aponeurosis angle, MT=muscle thickness and PA=pennation

angle. Fascicle length was reported in absolute terms (cm). The extrapolation measure and

equation has been validated against cadaveric BFlh tissue and is considered a robust way of

estimating fascicle lengths (25).The same assessor (RGT) collected and analysed all scans

and was blinded to participant identifiers during the analysis.

Once the movement commenced, participants were cued to keep their hips in a position of

Participants undertook a standardised warm up protocol consisting of one repetition at each

undertaken with the force plates (ForceDecks FD4000, Vald Performance, Queensland,

were required to lay supine, with the heel of the limb being tested positioned on top of the

         A significant main effect for group (p=0.009) and time (p=0.023) was also found for

over 40m when compared to the ISO group at the end of pre-season (Difference 0.110s, 95%

CI 0.006 to 0.214s, d = 0.87, p = 0.039). There were no other significant within or between

group changes in 40m sprint performance (d range = 0.03 to 0.72, p range = 0.085 to 0.993).

Horizontal force-velocity profile. A significant main effect for group (p=0.007) and time




 C
(p=0.021) was found for maximal horizontal velocity. Post hoc analyses found that the NHE

group had a significantly greater horizontal velocity than the ISO group at the end of pre-

season (Difference 0.26m/s, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.51m/s, d = 0.82, p = 0.049; Supplemental

Table 3, Supplemental Digital Content 3). There were no other significant within or between

group changes in horizontal force-velocity profiles (d range = 0.06 to 0.82, p range = 0.057 to

0.876)

 DISCUSSION

   This is the first study to investigate the impact of a long-term (38 week) NHE or isometric

knee flexor training intervention, alongside a periodised sprinting program, on BFlh

architecture, strength and sprinting performance in ARF athletes. The novel findings of this

study are:

   1. Undertaking a NHE or isometric knee flexor training intervention, alongside a

                                                                                  D
        periodised sprinting program, significantly improves BFlh fascicle length and muscle




                            EP
        thickness across 38 weeks.

   2. Both interventions also significantly increase eccentric strength across the in-season

        period, with no alterations during pre-season.




                              TE
   3. Isometric knee flexor strength significantly reduced at the end of both the pre-season

        for both groups, with the ISO group getting weaker in-season.

   4. Undertaking NHE training, alongside a periodised sprinting program, across a 14

        week pre-season period can significantly improve 5m split time, and


             C
   5. A NHE intervention, alongside a periodised sprinting program, can significantly




AC
        improve maximal sprinting velocity over 40m when compared to an ISO training

        intervention after a 14 week pre-season period.


   This is the first study to prescribe a single-mode hamstring specific exercise intervention,

alongside a periodised sprinting program, in semi-professional competitive athletes. Previous

research in this area is limited with its application to athletic populations as it has either

implemented a single exercise intervention in recreationally active participants (12, 13, 19,

31) or has not controlled and prescribed a periodised sprinting program as part of the training

prescription (11). The key inclusion of the periodised sprinting program alongside a single-




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 mode hamstring specific exercise intervention in this study allows for a more holistic and

translatable set of findings as it shows the outcomes when both are prescribed together, which

is commonplace in applied settings.



        Elite ARF athletes who possess short BFlh fascicles are more likely to suffer a HSI

than those who have longer fascicles (7). In a similar elite ARF cohort, possessing low levels

of eccentric knee flexor strength has also been shown to increase the likelihood of a HSI

                                                                                  D
occurring (32), although this is not a consistent finding (6, 7, 33). Whilst it is unknown if

modifications in these variables are associated with a change in the risk of HSI occurring,




                            EP
those who undertook the NHE intervention in the current study saw a 1.15cm (11%) and a

38N (9%) increase in fascicle length and eccentric strength across the study, respectively.




                              TE
Similarly, the ISO training group saw a 0.82cm (7%) and a 49N (12%) increase in both

fascicle length and eccentric strength respectively. The findings for the ISO training group in

the current study are the first to show that it is possible to increase BFlh fascicle length and

eccentric strength while undertaking a period of isometric training. However, the current



             C
study does differ compared to previous isometric hamstring training studies (17, 19). All

previous interventions have been undertaken using a single-exercise approach (17, 19),




A
whereas the current study includes a periodised sprinting program which was undertaken




 C
alongside the resistance training stimuli. As the BFlh is hypothesized to undergo significant

lengthening during sprinting (4), it is possible that the inclusion of the periodised sprinting

program may have contributed to the increases in BFlh fascicle length and eccentric strength

for both groups. There is also some evidence to support the idea that sprint training alone is

capable of increasing BFlh fascicle lengths (34). When considering these findings alongside

the prospective risk factor evidence for BFlh fascicle length and eccentric strength, it is

possible that completing NHE or ISO exercise alongside a periodised sprinting program may




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 have a beneficial effect on HSI risk mitigation, although this would require further

investigation.



        Muscle thickness of the BFlh was significantly increased after the pre-season period

in both groups. This is the first evidence that isometric training interventions can improve

muscle thickness in the BFlh (19), whereas NHE interventions have previously been shown

to increase muscle thickness (13, 34). Similar to the fascicle length improvements in the ISO

                                                                                  D
group, the inclusion of a sprint training stimulus in the current study may have contributed to

these improvements as a period of sprint only training has been shown to increase BFlh




                            EP
muscle thickness (34). These results suggest that training programs aiming at improving

muscle thickness and fascicle length of the BFlh could include either an eccentric or




                              TE
isometric resistance training stimuli alongside a periodised sprinting program.




        We found a significant reduction in isometric knee flexor strength for both groups at

the end of the intervention. An assessment of isometric knee flexor strength was included in

             C
the current study to assist in the detection of any contraction mode specific adaptations to the




A
two divergent training interventions. However, there are several factors which may need to be




 C
considered when interpreting these findings. It has been previously shown that there is a

joint-angle specificity for adaptations following isometric training interventions (35). As such

in the ISO group, the difference in joint position between the isometric strength testing (90°

hip and knee flexion) and training stimuli (approx. 45° at the knee and a neutral hip) may

have led to the reductions seen. The isometric strength testing position used in this study has

been previously shown as reliable when implemented in athletic populations (20). Previous

evidence has found no association between isometric strength and HSI risk (8), however this




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 assessment of isometric knee flexor strength is regularly used as part of screening batteries to

track athlete recovery (36) and training management as required (37). Considering the joint-

angle specificity of isometric training adaptations (35), it is possible that if we had tested

isometric knee flexor strength in the joint positions where it was trained, we may have seen

significant improvements in the ISO group. However, the assessment of isometric knee flexor

strength was chosen because of its proven reliability and its capacity to allow a greater

                                                                                  D
throughput when assessing individuals in an applied setting. Conversely, undertaking a




                            EP
period of eccentric training has been shown to improve eccentric but not isometric strength

(19). Therefore, whilst the testing position may have impacted the ability to see significant

increases in the ISO group, in the NHE group it may be a case of a contraction mode specific




                              TE
adaptation leading to the current findings. Considering these findings alongside the

methodological intricacies of the current study, future research should consider measuring

isometric strength at various joint positions in athletic cohorts to determine if there is a joint-

angle specificity to the adaptations seen following a period of isometric training.


             C
        In ARF, the evolution of the game has resulted in a significant increase of the number




A
of short-distance sprinting efforts (3). As a result, high performance programs aim to improve




 C
acceleration capacity (5m sprint performance) more than longer distance sprinting efforts

(e.g., over 30m) (38). In the current study, at the end of pre-season the NHE group had

significantly improved their 5m split time by 3.3%. To contextualise these findings in a

sporting context, an average participant from the NHE group may gain an extra 15 to 20cm

advantage across 5m when competing against an ISO group participant. In addition to this,

the NHE group also possessed a greater maximum velocity than the ISO group at the end of

the pre-season. In ARF this improvement may be crucial to improving an athlete’s ability to




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 best their opponent during contests (3). The improvement in a performance metric such as 5m

split time may also assist the “buy-in” and implementation of an exercise-based injury

prevention strategy in a high-performance setting where the balance between performance

and prevention is a key component of the role (39).



        There are limitations in the current study. The measurement of fascicle length from

the BFlh is an estimation made using an equation validated in comparison to cadaveric data

                                                                                  D
(24, 25). This estimation is required due to the small field of view being unable to capture the

entire fascicle. This methodology was chosen due to fascicle length measures using it have




                            EP
been prospectively associated injury (8). This technique has also been shown to be reliable

and have a high level of agreement with cadaveric samples (25). Minimal clinically




                              TE
importance difference values for the architectural or strength measures weren’t determined as

no previous interventions have directly investigated whether changes in fascicle length or

eccentric strength are associated with a reduction in injury incidence. Finally, there was no

control group and as such we were unable to determine the impact that ARF or sprint training



             C
alone would have on the outcome measures. However, this is the first study to prescribe a

periodised sprinting program alongside a single-exercise intervention to ensure that as much




A
of the stimuli related to hamstring adaptation were controlled.




 C
CONCLUSIONS

        In conclusion, undertaking an NHE or isometric knee flexor training intervention

alongside a periodised sprinting program appears to improve fascicle length, muscle

thickness and eccentric knee flexor strength in ARF athletes. Whereas isometric knee flexor

strength appears to decline with either intervention, although this could be due to joint angle

or contraction mode specific adaptations. Additionally, undertaking a NHE training




    Copyright © 2023 by the American College of Sports Medicine. Unauthorized reproduction of this article is prohibited.
 intervention, alongside a periodised sprinting program, significantly improves acceleration

capacity and maximum velocity. These findings provide unique, contextually relevant

insights into the adaptations that may be possible in trained athletes.

903	                           3.2. Evidence Quality and Data Collection Methods
904	                                 Using the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics Quality Criteria Checklist: Primary Research
905	                           tool (Supplementary Table S2), 21 of the 35 studies were rated as positive primary research
906	                           studies [37,40,54–60,62–66,70,73,79,80,82,84,85]. Thirteen studies were rated as neutral, as they
907	                           did not satisfy all required criteria (criterion 2, 3, 6, and 7) [43,61,67–69,71,72,75–78,81,83]. One
908	                           study was rated as negative, as this studied satisfied only three of the 10 validity questions [74].
909	                           Although the majority of studies were classed as positive based on the criteria [53], many studies
910	                           provided inadequate information surrounding withdrawal and attrition rates of their partici-
911	                           pants [37,40,43,54,55,57,59,65–72,74,76], and seven studies measuring only subjective sleep out-
912	                           comes did not use validated sleep tools [67,69,71,72,76,77,83], six studies provided limited infor-
913	                           mation or used inappropriate statistical methods for the study design [67,71,74–76,82], five studies
914	                           had concerns around blinding of participants and/or researchers [40,55,63,70,74], two studies
915	                           did not discuss the limitations of their studies [71,74], and two did not report randomization
916	                           techniques used for participant condition assignment [74,75]. Most neutral rated studies satisfied
917	                           the majority of criteria outside of criterion two (assessing selection bias).
918	                                 Sixteen studies objectively recorded sleep [37,40,43,54–61,63–66,73], with 19 providing only
919	                           subjective measures of sleep [62,67–72,74–85]. Three studies recorded sleep via polysomnogra-
920	                           phy (PSG) [57,61,63], and 13 through actigraphy [37,40,43,54–56,58–60,64–66,73]. Of those that
921	                           used actigraphy, 8% (n = 1) used a high sleep-wake threshold (>80 activity counts) [65], 23% (n
922	                           = 3) a medium threshold (>40 activity counts) [37,54,59], 8% (n = 1) used the Cole–Kripke algo-
923	                           rithm [43], and 15% (n = 2) used the ‘Readiband’ device-specific software [58,64]. The sleep-wake
924	                           threshold/algorithm was not reported by 46% (n = 6) of studies using actigraphy [40,55,56,60,66,
925	                           73]. The most common subjective sleep data collection tools included the Pittsburgh Sleep Qual-
926	                           ity Index (n = 8) [62,74,78–82,85], Epworth Sleepiness Scale (n = 4) [40,61,62,81], sleep quality
927	                           rated on a 1–5 scale (n = 4) [65,70,72,75], and the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (n = 3) [43,60,80].
928	
929	                           3.3. Qualitative Synthesis
930	                           3.3.1. Macronutrients and Energy
931	                           Carbohydrates
932	                                 Five studies assessed the influence of carbohydrates on the sleep of athletic populations
933	                           (Table 2) [37,40,55–57]. Two studies investigated the influence of GI on sleep [40,57]. In
934	                           recreationally-trained individuals, a high GI meal consumed immediately post-evening
935	                           exercise increased PSG derived total sleep time (+1 h) and sleep efficiency (+8.1%), and
936	                           reduced sleep latency (−18.9 min) and WASO (−32.9 min) compared to a low GI meal [57].
937	                           Contrasting this, the sleep of state-level basketballers was unaffected by the GI of the
938	                           evening meal and snack they consumed [40].
939	                                 Following 10 consecutive days of diet and sleep tracking via actigraphy, the sleep of
940	                           elite male Australian footballers was associated with carbohydrate timing (Table 2) [37]. To-
941	                           tal daily carbohydrate intake (mean 3.4 ± 1.4 g·kg·d−1 ) was not associated with sleep; how-
942	                           ever, for every 1 g·kg−1 increase in evening (post 6 pm) sugar intake, there was an associated
943	                           reduction of TST by five minutes (p = 0.027), increase in sleep efficiency of 0.2% (p = 0.021),
944	                           and a decrease in WASO by one minute (p = 0.005). In elite female Australian footballers,
945	                           however, total daily carbohydrate intake (mean 3.3 ± 1.3 g·kg·d−1 ) was associated with
946	                           impaired sleep [54]. For every 1 g·kg−1 increase in total daily carbohydrate intake, there
947	                           was an associated reduction in sleep efficiency by 0.6% (p = 0.007), and an increase in WASO
948	                           by 3.6 min (p = 0.007). Further, in trained triathletes, a three-week sleep-low carbohydrate
949	                           intervention slightly reduced sleep efficiency by 1.1% (p < 0.05) compared to a control diet,
950	                           with no other sleep metrics affected [55]. This sleep-low strategy referred to carbohydrate
951	                           availability, with the sleep-low group having carbohydrate intake restricted throughout
952	                           exercise and dinner, resulting in low carbohydrate availability at rest (Table 2). Similarly, a
953	                           10-day high carbohydrate intervention (9.9 ± 1.5 g·kg·d−1 vs. 7.4 ± 1.6 g·kg·d−1 ) within
954	                           highly-trained male cyclists resulted in minimal influences on sleep, with total sleep time
955	                           slightly decreased (0.3 h) compared to control (p = 0.03) [56]. This 10-day period involved
956	                           a 1.5-fold increase in typical training volume, which was independently associated with
