965	                           Protein
966	                                 One three-armed crossover trial investigated the influence of protein type (cottage
967	                           cheese, casein, and placebo) on the sleep of 10 active females (Table 2) [58]. The cottage
968	                           cheese and casein contained 30 g of protein and 10 g carbohydrates, with the placebo being
969	                           non-nutritive. These foods were consumed 30–60 min before bed for one night, and did
970	                           not influence actigraphy derived total sleep time, sleep latency, or sleep efficiency across
971	                           intervention groups. These findings were similar to a 10-day prospective cohort study
972	                           of elite female Australian footballers, whereby a mean intake of 1.8 ± 0.6 g·kg·d−1 body
973	                           weight of protein was not associated with sleep. This differed to a cohort study of elite male
974	                           Australian footballers, with increases in total daily and evening protein intake associated
975	                           with multiple sleep metrics tracked through actigraphy. Every 1-g·kg−1 increase in daily
976	                           protein intake (mean 2.2 ± 0.8 g·kg·d−1 ) related to a decreased sleep efficiency of 0.7%
977	                           (p = 0.006) and an increased WASO of four minutes (p = 0.013), whereas each 1 g·kg−1
978	                           increase in evening protein intake was associated with a reduction of sleep latency by
979	                           two minutes (p = 0.013) [37].
980	
981	                           Whey Protein and Alpha-Lactalbumin
982	                                Four studies have objectively measured the sleep of athletically trained popula-
983	                           tions post-evening consumption of protein sources rich in the amino acid tryptophan
984	                           (Table 2) [43,59–61]. One crossover study that supplemented elite male Australian foot-
985	                           ballers with 55 g of whey protein (containing 1-g TRP) or an isocaloric placebo on a training
986	                           and non-training day observed no effect on sleep [59].
987	                                Three studies investigated the impact of α-lactalbumin supplementation [43,60,61]—
988	                           the richest food source of TRP [86]—on sleep. Most sleep metrics measured across the
989	                           three studies were unaffected following 40–60 g α-lactalbumin (containing 2–3 g TRP)
990	                           supplemented two hours before bed for 2–3 nights. Total sleep time ranged across these
991	                           studies from 6.9 to 7.7 h, sleep latency from 2 to 25 min, sleep efficiency between 87.2 and
992	                           90.5%, and WASO between 38 and 48 min across all experimental groups [43,60,61]. The
993	                           two studies that observed no changes in sleep were measured via actigraphy [43,60], whilst
994	                           a significant increase in N-REM stage 2 sleep was observed in trained females following PSG
995	                           measurement [61]. Additionally, these females completed a simulated evening competition
996	                           (18:30–20:00) prior to supplementation and sleep.
997	
998	                           Fats
999	                                Two prospective cohort studies of elite Australian footballers investigated the influence
1000	                           of macronutrients on sleep across a 10 day period in the preseason [37,54]. In male Australian
1001	                           footballers, dietary fat intake (mean 1.7 ± 0.7 g·kg·d−1 ) was not associated with sleep [37]. In
1002	                           female Australian footballers, however, increases in saturated fat intake was associated with
1003	                           reductions in actigraphy measured sleep latency [54]. For every 1-g increase in saturated fat
1004	                           intake, there was an associated reduction of sleep latency by 0.27 min (p = 0.030).
1005	
1006	                           Energy
1007	                                In a study of 67 international level rhythmic gymnasts, 82% were found to consume
1008	                           <2000 kCal·d−1 (Table 2) [62]. There were no differences identified between the subjective
1009	                           sleep quality, duration, or daytime sleepiness in gymnasts consuming either <2000 kCal·d−1
1010	                           or ≥2000 kCal·d−1 , as assessed through the PSQI and Epworth Sleepiness Scale [62].
1011	                           One female cohort study of Australian footballers similarly found no association between
1012	                           daily energy intake (mean 9347 ± 2905 kJ (~2234 kCal)) and sleep, whereas two studies of
1013	                           male athletes presented contrasting findings. A prospective study of 36 elite Australian
1014	                           male footballers observed that increases in daily energy intake (mean 14000 ± 4000 kJ
1015	                           (~3346 kCal)) were significantly associated with actigraphy-derived measures of sleep

                           3.2. Evidence Quality and Data Collection Methods
                                 Using the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics Quality Criteria Checklist: Primary Research
                           tool (Supplementary Table S2), 21 of the 35 studies were rated as positive primary research
                           studies [37,40,54–60,62–66,70,73,79,80,82,84,85]. Thirteen studies were rated as neutral, as they
                           did not satisfy all required criteria (criterion 2, 3, 6, and 7) [43,61,67–69,71,72,75–78,81,83]. One
                           study was rated as negative, as this studied satisfied only three of the 10 validity questions [74].
                           Although the majority of studies were classed as positive based on the criteria [53], many studies
                           provided inadequate information surrounding withdrawal and attrition rates of their partici-
                           pants [37,40,43,54,55,57,59,65–72,74,76], and seven studies measuring only subjective sleep out-
                           comes did not use validated sleep tools [67,69,71,72,76,77,83], six studies provided limited infor-
                           mation or used inappropriate statistical methods for the study design [67,71,74–76,82], five studies
                           had concerns around blinding of participants and/or researchers [40,55,63,70,74], two studies
                           did not discuss the limitations of their studies [71,74], and two did not report randomization
                           techniques used for participant condition assignment [74,75]. Most neutral rated studies satisfied
                           the majority of criteria outside of criterion two (assessing selection bias).
                                 Sixteen studies objectively recorded sleep [37,40,43,54–61,63–66,73], with 19 providing only
                           subjective measures of sleep [62,67–72,74–85]. Three studies recorded sleep via polysomnogra-
                           phy (PSG) [57,61,63], and 13 through actigraphy [37,40,43,54–56,58–60,64–66,73]. Of those that
                           used actigraphy, 8% (n = 1) used a high sleep-wake threshold (>80 activity counts) [65], 23% (n
                           = 3) a medium threshold (>40 activity counts) [37,54,59], 8% (n = 1) used the Cole–Kripke algo-
                           rithm [43], and 15% (n = 2) used the ‘Readiband’ device-specific software [58,64]. The sleep-wake
                           threshold/algorithm was not reported by 46% (n = 6) of studies using actigraphy [40,55,56,60,66,
                           73]. The most common subjective sleep data collection tools included the Pittsburgh Sleep Qual-
                           ity Index (n = 8) [62,74,78–82,85], Epworth Sleepiness Scale (n = 4) [40,61,62,81], sleep quality
                           rated on a 1–5 scale (n = 4) [65,70,72,75], and the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (n = 3) [43,60,80].

                           3.3. Qualitative Synthesis
                           3.3.1. Macronutrients and Energy
                           Carbohydrates
                                 Five studies assessed the influence of carbohydrates on the sleep of athletic populations
                           (Table 2) [37,40,55–57]. Two studies investigated the influence of GI on sleep [40,57]. In
                           recreationally-trained individuals, a high GI meal consumed immediately post-evening
                           exercise increased PSG derived total sleep time (+1 h) and sleep efficiency (+8.1%), and
                           reduced sleep latency (−18.9 min) and WASO (−32.9 min) compared to a low GI meal [57].
                           Contrasting this, the sleep of state-level basketballers was unaffected by the GI of the
                           evening meal and snack they consumed [40].
                                 Following 10 consecutive days of diet and sleep tracking via actigraphy, the sleep of
                           elite male Australian footballers was associated with carbohydrate timing (Table 2) [37]. To-
                           tal daily carbohydrate intake (mean 3.4 ± 1.4 g·kg·d−1 ) was not associated with sleep; how-
                           ever, for every 1 g·kg−1 increase in evening (post 6 pm) sugar intake, there was an associated
                           reduction of TST by five minutes (p = 0.027), increase in sleep efficiency of 0.2% (p = 0.021),
                           and a decrease in WASO by one minute (p = 0.005). In elite female Australian footballers,
                           however, total daily carbohydrate intake (mean 3.3 ± 1.3 g·kg·d−1 ) was associated with
                           impaired sleep [54]. For every 1 g·kg−1 increase in total daily carbohydrate intake, there
                           was an associated reduction in sleep efficiency by 0.6% (p = 0.007), and an increase in WASO
                           by 3.6 min (p = 0.007). Further, in trained triathletes, a three-week sleep-low carbohydrate
                           intervention slightly reduced sleep efficiency by 1.1% (p < 0.05) compared to a control diet,
                           with no other sleep metrics affected [55]. This sleep-low strategy referred to carbohydrate
                           availability, with the sleep-low group having carbohydrate intake restricted throughout
                           exercise and dinner, resulting in low carbohydrate availability at rest (Table 2). Similarly, a
                           10-day high carbohydrate intervention (9.9 ± 1.5 g·kg·d−1 vs. 7.4 ± 1.6 g·kg·d−1 ) within
                           highly-trained male cyclists resulted in minimal influences on sleep, with total sleep time
                           slightly decreased (0.3 h) compared to control (p = 0.03) [56]. This 10-day period involved

                           an increase of six wake bouts (p = 0.03) and a five percent reduction in sleep efficiency
                           (p < 0.05).

                           Protein
                                 One three-armed crossover trial investigated the influence of protein type (cottage
                           cheese, casein, and placebo) on the sleep of 10 active females (Table 2) [58]. The cottage
                           cheese and casein contained 30 g of protein and 10 g carbohydrates, with the placebo being
                           non-nutritive. These foods were consumed 30–60 min before bed for one night, and did
                           not influence actigraphy derived total sleep time, sleep latency, or sleep efficiency across
                           intervention groups. These findings were similar to a 10-day prospective cohort study
                           of elite female Australian footballers, whereby a mean intake of 1.8 ± 0.6 g·kg·d−1 body
                           weight of protein was not associated with sleep. This differed to a cohort study of elite male
                           Australian footballers, with increases in total daily and evening protein intake associated
                           with multiple sleep metrics tracked through actigraphy. Every 1-g·kg−1 increase in daily
                           protein intake (mean 2.2 ± 0.8 g·kg·d−1 ) related to a decreased sleep efficiency of 0.7%
                           (p = 0.006) and an increased WASO of four minutes (p = 0.013), whereas each 1 g·kg−1
                           increase in evening protein intake was associated with a reduction of sleep latency by
                           two minutes (p = 0.013) [37].

                           Whey Protein and Alpha-Lactalbumin
                                Four studies have objectively measured the sleep of athletically trained popula-
                           tions post-evening consumption of protein sources rich in the amino acid tryptophan
                           (Table 2) [43,59–61]. One crossover study that supplemented elite male Australian foot-
                           ballers with 55 g of whey protein (containing 1-g TRP) or an isocaloric placebo on a training
                           and non-training day observed no effect on sleep [59].
                                Three studies investigated the impact of α-lactalbumin supplementation [43,60,61]—
                           the richest food source of TRP [86]—on sleep. Most sleep metrics measured across the
                           three studies were unaffected following 40–60 g α-lactalbumin (containing 2–3 g TRP)
                           supplemented two hours before bed for 2–3 nights. Total sleep time ranged across these
                           studies from 6.9 to 7.7 h, sleep latency from 2 to 25 min, sleep efficiency between 87.2 and
                           90.5%, and WASO between 38 and 48 min across all experimental groups [43,60,61]. The
                           two studies that observed no changes in sleep were measured via actigraphy [43,60], whilst
                           a significant increase in N-REM stage 2 sleep was observed in trained females following PSG
                           measurement [61]. Additionally, these females completed a simulated evening competition
                           (18:30–20:00) prior to supplementation and sleep.

                           Fats
                                Two prospective cohort studies of elite Australian footballers investigated the influence
                           of macronutrients on sleep across a 10 day period in the preseason [37,54]. In male Australian
                           footballers, dietary fat intake (mean 1.7 ± 0.7 g·kg·d−1 ) was not associated with sleep [37]. In
                           female Australian footballers, however, increases in saturated fat intake was associated with
                           reductions in actigraphy measured sleep latency [54]. For every 1-g increase in saturated fat
                           intake, there was an associated reduction of sleep latency by 0.27 min (p = 0.030).

                           Energy
                                In a study of 67 international level rhythmic gymnasts, 82% were found to consume
                           <2000 kCal·d−1 (Table 2) [62]. There were no differences identified between the subjective
                           sleep quality, duration, or daytime sleepiness in gymnasts consuming either <2000 kCal·d−1
                           or ≥2000 kCal·d−1 , as assessed through the PSQI and Epworth Sleepiness Scale [62].
                           One female cohort study of Australian footballers similarly found no association between
                           daily energy intake (mean 9347 ± 2905 kJ (~2234 kCal)) and sleep, whereas two studies of
                           male athletes presented contrasting findings. A prospective study of 36 elite Australian
                           male footballers observed that increases in daily energy intake (mean 14000 ± 4000 kJ
                           (~3346 kCal)) were significantly associated with actigraphy-derived measures of sleep

1028	                                One cohort study of elite female Australian footballers investigated the impact of
1029	                           habitual micronutrient intake within the preseason on sleep (Table 2) [54]. Sleep was
1030	                           measured via actigraphy, with associations between micronutrients and sleep reported
1031	                           per unit increase in micronutrient consumption. A longer TST was associated with higher
1032	                           iron intake (per 1 mg, 0.55 min); an increased sleep efficiency was associated with higher

1035	                           magnesium intake (per 1 mg, 0.02 min); a reduction in WASO was associated with higher
1036	                           vitamin B12 intake (per 1 µg, 1.72 min); whereas a reduction in TST was associated with
1037	                           higher sodium intake (per 1 mg, 0.012 min); and a reduction in sleep efficiency was
1038	                           associated with higher vitamin E intake (per 1 mg, 0.08%).

1040	                           3.3.3. Dietary Supplementation
1041	                           Caffeine
1042	                                Eight studies investigated the impact of caffeine on sleep [63–69,84], with all studies
1043	                           observing a negative effect on either sleep duration and/or quality (Table 3). Most studies
1044	                           had participants consume caffeine before evening exercise (e.g., ≥5 p.m.), with intake
1045	                           ranging from 45–75 min pre-session [63–69]. One study supplemented participants with
1046	                           caffeine prior to a morning swimming trial (09:00–11:30 am) [67]. Four studies objectively
1047	                           measured sleep [63–66], with evening caffeine intake ranging from ~2 to 6 mg·kg−1 body
1048	                           mass (Table 3). Three studies observed reductions in total sleep time (−1.2–2.8 h) [63,64,66]
1049	                           and sleep efficiency (−5.8–15.4%) [63–65], and an increased sleep latency (+7.8–40.9 min) [63,
1050	                           64,66]. Wake after sleep onset was increased in two studies (+22.9–33.2 min) [63,65], with
1051	                           an increase of 5.3 awakenings observed in another study following caffeine conditions [65].
1052	                           Compared to placebo, caffeine conditions negatively affected subjective measures of sleep
1053	                           including total sleep time [67], sleep latency [65,67,68], sleep quality [65,68], and prevalence
1054	                           of insomnia [69] across multiple studies. In endurance athletes, consuming ≤1.5 cups of
1055	                           caffeinated beverages per day was associated with a significantly better sleep quality and a
1056	                           lower sleep difficulty (p < 0.05) as assessed via the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire
1057	                           (ASSQ) [84].
1058	
1059	                           Cherry Juice
1060	                                Using subjective measures, two studies explored the impact of cherry juice on the sleep
1061	                           of athletes [70,71]. In professional rugby league athletes, supplementation of 2 × 30 mL
1062	                           Montmorency cherry juice (morning and night) for eight days had no influence on subjective
1063	                           sleep quality, as measured via a 1–5 Likert Scale (Table 3) [70]. In contrast, a survey
1064	                           of 80 ≥ sub-elite athletes revealed that 14% of the athletes who had previously or are
1065	                           currently supplementing a non-specified amount of tart cherry juice reported improved
1066	                           sleep (Table 3) [71]. The general questionnaire used did not specify the type of sleep
1067	                           improvement experienced, so it is unknown whether 14% of these athletes experienced
1068	                           improvements in sleep quality or duration.
1069	
1070	                           Pre and Probiotics
1071	                                Two randomized control trials supplemented professional rugby union or soccer play-
1072	                           ers with probiotics and measured sleep outcomes for a period of 30 days to 17 weeks
1073	                           (Table 3) [72,73]. Following 30 days supplementation of a 300-mg mixture of probi-
1074	                           otic (Bifidobacterium lactis, Bifidobacterium longum, and Lactobacillus rhamnosus) and pre-

1076	
1077	
1078

1080	                           biotic (fructooligosaccharides) strains, actigraphy-derived measures of sleep latency and
1081	                           sleep efficiency were improved in Spanish soccer players by 0.5 min and 3.3%, respec-
1082	                           tively [73]. Further, bi-daily supplementation of a proprietary probiotic blend (Lactobacillus,
1083	                           Bifidobacterium, and Streptococcus), improved the subjective sleep quality of professional
1084	                           Australian rugby union players compared to placebo [72]. Athletes were studied for 17
1085	                           weeks in-season, with eight weeks domestic competition and nine weeks of international
1086	                           competition. The probiotic group were supplemented with an additional two SBFlorac-
1087	                           tiv™ (Saccharomyces boulardii) probiotic capsules daily during international travel to limit
1088	                           traveller’s diarrhoea, which the placebo group did not receive.
1089	
1090	                           Other Dietary Supplements
1091	                                Male athletes supplemented with 100 mL of beetroot juice (300 mg nitrates) two hours
1092	                           pre-exercise (exercise timing not reported) for seven days, significantly improved subjective
1093	                           sleep quality compared to placebo (Table 3) [74]. The PSQI global score of the athletes
1094	                           in the beetroot juice group was reduced by more than half from baseline (14.5–5.8) [74].
1095	                           This study was reviewed as being negative quality, given the lack of information around
1096	                           participants, interventions (i.e., exercise type and timing, dietary controls) and reporting
1097	                           of data. In professional rugby union males, the addition of 1546 mg omega-3 to protein
1098	                           shakes consumed after a morning and afternoon exercise session had no effect on subjective
1099	                           sleep quality compared to placebo [75]. Similarly, acute supplementation of chocolate milk
1100	                           (12 g protein, 30 g carbohydrates) in trained female runners and triathletes did not influence
1101	                           subjective total sleep time compared to placebo [76]. Lastly, a cross-sectional survey conducted
1102	                           with 517 elite male rugby players displayed that 41% of athletes that were currently or had
1103	                           previously supplemented undefined amounts of cannabidiol (CBD) experienced improved
1104	                           sleep [77]. As no defined CBD amount was included, the dose required to elicit a positive
1105	                           influence on sleep in athletically trained populations remains unknown.
1106	
1107	                           3.3.4. Dietary Patterns
1108	                           Meal Timing and Patterns
1109	                                Four cross-sectional survey-based studies and one prospective cohort study explored
1110	                           the associations between meal timing on sleep duration and/or quality (Table 4) [78–81].
1111	                           These four cross-sectional studies measured sleep quality via the PSQI, and involved
1112	                           populations including student athletes [78], visually-impaired athletes [79], and elite ath-
1113	                           letes [80,81]. Two studies of student and Paralympic athletes observed no influence of
1114	                           meal timing on subjective sleep quality [78,79]. In contrast, regression analysis displayed
1115	                           an association with eating breakfast every morning and sleep quality (p < 0.01) in elite
1116	                           athletes [81], and eating a heavy meal within three hours of bed related to a subjective
1117	                           increase in total sleep time (p < 0.05) and WASO (p < 0.05) in youth athletes [80]. This
1118	                           contrasts the findings of Falkenberg et al. [37], whereby every additional hour between
1119	                           the main evening meal and bedtime was associated with a decrease in sleep duration by
1120	                           eight minutes (p = 0.042), and a decrease in WASO by two minutes (p = 0.015) in Australian
1121	                           footballers [37]. Further, an eight-week three-armed randomized control trial observed
1122	                           no significant changes in the PSQI global score of resistance trained females following a
1123	                           control diet or a time-restricted feeding protocol (all calories consumed between 12:00 h
1124	                           and 20:00 h) with and without 3 g·d−1 β-hydroxy β-methylbutyrate supplementation [85].
1125	
1126	                           Total Diet
1127	                                A survey-based study of female college athletes investigated the relationship between
1128	                           food and nutrient intake on sleep quality (Table 4) [82]. Using PSQI global scores, ath-
1129	                           letes were categorized as either being no-risk (score < 5.5) or at-risk for sleep disorders
1130	                           (score ≥ 5.5). As measured via the Food Intake Frequency Questionnaire (Japanese version),
1131	                           there was no significant differences in any nutrient or food group intake between the no-risk
1132	                           or at-risk groups, except for a higher bean intake in the at-risk for sleep disorder group

1134

1139	                           no significant influence of wholegrain, fruit, and vegetable consumption on sleep difficulty.
1140	
1141	                           Dairy Consumption
1142	                                 In elite female athletes, a medium to high frequency of milk consumption (>3 days
1143	                           per week) was associated with a lower risk of reduced subjective sleep quality (OR = 0.38,
1144	                           p < 0.001) [83]. Sleep quality was rated on a 1–3 scale, with participant’s intake of dairy and
1145	                           milk categorized as either low, medium, or high. There were no associations between the
1146	                           frequency of milk or dairy consumption on male athlete sleep quality, or total sleep time
1147	                           for either sex (Table 4). Similarly in endurance athletes, dairy consumption was not related
1148	                           to sleep difficulty or quality as assessed via the ASSQ [84].
1149	
1150	                           4. Discussion
1151	                                  This is the first systematic review to evaluate the available evidence on the impact of
1152	                           multiple dietary factors on the sleep of athletically trained populations. Consistent with
1153	                           literature in non-athlete populations, results from the 35 studies examined suggests that
1154	                           dietary factors may influence the sleep of athletically trained populations. The main findings
1155	                           from this systematic review were that: macronutrient timing (i.e., evening) and composition
1156	                           (i.e., carbohydrate GI) appear to have a stronger influence on sleep than total daily macronu-
1157	                           trient consumption; caffeine consumed before evening exercise negatively impacts sleep; and,
1158	                           sustained probiotic supplementation may promote sleep. These findings can help formulate
1159	                           sports nutrition guidelines to promote sleep in athletically trained populations.
1160	                                  The impact of protein on sleep varied between sexes. In elite male Australian foot-
1161	                           ballers, high protein intake was associated with a lower sleep efficiency and an increased
1162	                           WASO [37]; however, there was no effect of protein on the sleep of their elite female
1163	                           counterparts [54]. Though the effect of protein on sleep efficiency and WASO in the
1164	                           male footballers was small and unlikely meaningful, the discrepancy observed between
1165	                           these studies may be explained by the higher protein intakes of the male footballers
1166	                           (2.2 g·kg·d−1 vs. 1.8 g·kg·d−1 ), or by the type and timing of the protein consumed. Amino
1167	                           acid composition of meals were not assessed in either study; however, the male footballers
1168	                           frequently reported consumption of whey protein in the evening, with evening protein
1169	                           intake associated with reductions in sleep latency. Four studies within this review investi-
1170	                           gated the relationship between sleep and evening protein supplementation rich in trypto-
1171	                           phan [43,59–61]—a soporific amino acid that is a precursor to melatonin production [28,32].
1172	                           Alpha-lactalbumin is the second most predominant protein in whey, containing the highest
1173	                           tryptophan content of food protein sources [36,86]. One study that supplemented male
1174	                           Australian footballers with 55 g of whey protein (containing 1 g tryptophan) in the evening
1175	                           showed no effect on sleep [37]. This same tryptophan content is contained within ~20 g of
1176	                           pure α-lactalbumin [86], meaning the additional 35 g of whey protein required to reach this
1177	                           content may have contributed excessive amounts of LNAA in order to favour TRP avail-
1178	                           ability to the brain. Though it is well established that supplementation of α-lactalbumin
1179	                           increases the TRP:LNAA ratio [36,87–89], two studies examining well-trained male cyclists
1180	                           observed no beneficial effect of α-lactalbumin on sleep [43,60]. However, the average
1181	                           sleep efficiency across these two studies was >87% [43,60], and sleep latency was <3 min
1182	                           in one study [60], and previous research suggests that the sedative effects of TRP-based
1183	                           supplementation were less beneficial in populations without sleep complaints [32]. In
1184	                           contrast, α-lactalbumin supplementation improved the sleep of trained females [61], where
1185	                           sleep was measured following evening competition—a typically challenging sleep period
1186	                           for athletes [20]. Although an increase in N-REM 2 sleep was observed in the trained
1187	                           female study, a mixed meal (>24 g protein) was consumed alongside the 40-g α-lactalbumin
1188	                           supplement [61], which likely increased LNAA intake and potentially confounded the
1189	                           effects of the supplement on the TRP:LNAA ratio [38]. This same concept may explain the
1190	                           negative influence total daily protein intake had on sleep, as most protein sources are high
1191	                           in LNAAs and low in TRP [32,34]. Further research into the effects of α-lactalbumin on
1192	 Nutrients 2022, 14, 3271                                                                                          19 of 25
1193	
1194	
1195	
1196	
1197	                           the sleep of athletically trained populations should aim to recruit individuals with sleep
1198	                           difficulties, and isolate supplementation from mixed meals to limit confounding effects on
1199	                           the TRP:LNAA ratio. With protein requirements increased in athletic populations, further
1200	                           investigation of practical dietary strategies that reduce the impact of high protein intake on
1201	                           athlete sleep (i.e., manipulating protein type and timing) is necessary.
1202	                                 The timing and type of carbohydrates appears influential on sleep. The evening in-
1203	                           take of high GI carbohydrates was associated with improvements in sleep latency, WASO,
1204	                           and sleep efficiency in two studies of athletically trained populations [37,57]. In a double-
1205	                           randomized crossover study of recreationally trained males, consumption of a high GI meal
1206	                           (containing 2 g·kg−1 carbohydrates) immediately post evening sprint exercises increased
1207	                           total sleep time and sleep efficiency, and decreased WASO and sleep latency compared to a
1208	                           low GI meal as measured by polysomnography [57]. In contrast, within state-level basket-
1209	                           ballers, no influence on sleep was observed following evening consumption of high GI or
1210	                           low GI carbohydrate-based meals [40]. In addition to exercise being in the morning opposed
1211	                           to evening, this study of basketballers provided meals high in protein (64–81 g), which may
1212	                           have impacted the TRP:LNAA ratio [34,38]. Carbohydrates promote TRP availability to
1213	                           the brain through the action of insulin [34,35], but when included as part of a mixed meal
1214	                           containing high amounts of LNAAs and low TRP, the TRP:LNAA ratio is reduced [38].
1215	                           Increases in carbohydrate intake were associated with an increased WASO and decreased
1216	                           sleep efficiency in female Australian footballers; however, carbohydrate type was not as-
1217	                           sessed [54]. Previous research in a non-athletic female population does, however, indicate
1218	                           that high GI diets may increase insomnia risk [90]. With many athletes recommended to
1219	                           adopt high carbohydrate diets to maximize performance and recovery [91], it remains
1220	                           unknown whether there is a trade-off between daily carbohydrate intake, performance, and
1221	                           sleep. This displays the need for more research to determine the impact that carbohydrate
1222	                           type, timing, and total daily amounts have on the sleep of athletic populations, especially
1223	                           for females.
1224	                                 Caffeine inhibits athlete sleep, with doses ≤6 mg·kg−1 body mass affecting numer-
1225	                           ous sleep measures [63–69]. The influence of caffeine on sleep is well-established [92];
1226	                           however, the evidence-base within athletic populations has yet to be consolidated. To
1227	                           achieve the maximal ergogenic benefits of caffeine, it is recommended that caffeine be
1228	                           consumed at doses of 3–6 mg·kg−1 body mass 60 min prior to exercise [93]. Caffeine
1229	                           acutely enhances multiple aspects of performance, with increases in vigilance and aware-
1230	                           ness resulting from caffeine’s inhibitory action on adenosine receptors within the brain [94].
1231	                           This sleep-inhibiting action remains after exercise, with caffeine consumption prior to
1232	                           evening exercise resulting in more disrupted sleep [63–66,68,69]. Consuming caffeine at
1233	                           doses of 5 g·kg−1 of body mass may impair sleep quantity and quality for up to seven
1234	                           hours post consumption in athletes [67]. This aligns with previous data [95], whereby
1235	                           significant sleep disturbances have been observed in healthy adults consuming 400 mg of
1236	                           caffeine six hours prior to bedtime [95]. According to pharmacological data, the average
1237	                           half-life of caffeine is 4–6 h [96], meaning the continued stimulatory effect of caffeine on
1238	                           sleep is dependent on dosage and timing. This is highlighted by the habitual game day use
1239	                           of caffeine (~2 mg·kg−1 ) in Super Rugby athletes prior to evening competition, whereby
1240	                           caffeine consumed ~50 min before the match resulted in a decreased sleep duration and
1241	                           sleep efficiency, and greater difficulty falling asleep [64]. Knowledge that caffeine impairs
1242	                           athlete sleep for a considerable time post-ingestion allows athletes and practitioners to
1243	                           determine whether the benefits of caffeine on performance outweighs likely disrupted and
1244	                           poorer quality sleep following evening competition and training. Given the large number
1245	                           of athletes supplementing caffeine before evening training and competition, additional next
1246	                           day sleep opportunities should be provided following night-time caffeine supplementation
1247	                           to compensate for likely poorer sleep (i.e., no early morning recovery sessions, adjusting
1248	                           travel schedules to allow for more sleep, etc.).
1249	                                 Chronic probiotic supplementation may improve both objective and subjective sleep
1250	                           measures [72,73]. In professional soccer and rugby players, probiotic supplementation
1251	 Nutrients 2022, 14, 3271                                                                                           20 of 25
1252	
1253	
1254	
1255	
1256	                           resulted in improvements of multiple sleep metrics [72,73]. Though results are promis-
1257	                           ing, there are limitations to both studies. In soccer players supplemented with a mixture
1258	                           of probiotic strains for 30 days, sleep latency values were under two minutes [73]. This
1259	                           may indicate that athletes either had a significant accumulation of sleep debt [97], or that
1260	                           sleep latency values were underreported via actigraphy, a sleep tool with a potential small
1261	                           bias of ~9.5 min when measuring sleep latency [98]. Actigraphy may, therefore, not be
1262	                           sensitive enough to detect meaningful changes in sleep latency within athletes without
1263	                           sleep difficulties. Further, within the 17-week probiotic study of professional rugby union
1264	                           players, an additional bi-daily probiotic was supplemented only to the treatment group
1265	                           during international periods of the study (nine weeks) to prevent traveller’s diarrhea [72].
1266	                           The additional travelling probiotic may have confounded the relationship between the
1267	                           experimental probiotic and sleep [72]. Nevertheless, probiotic supplementation is seen
1268	                           to improve subjective sleep quality in non-athletic populations [99], including healthy fe-
1269	                           males [100], and individuals with chronic fatigue [101], chronic pain [102], and stress [103].
1270	                           Proposed mechanisms by which probiotics may elicit sleep benefits for athletes is through
1271	                           reducing muscle soreness via anti-inflammatory actions [72,104], and through their role in
1272	                           the synthesis of neuropeptides involved in the sleep/wake cycle, including melatonin [105].
1273	                           Although the preliminary research of probiotics and athlete’s sleep appears hopeful, further
1274	                           studies using more comprehensive means of objective sleep assessment (i.e., polysomnog-
1275	                           raphy) and stricter controls of confounding factors (e.g., dietary standardization, travel
1276	                           probiotics) are required to determine the true effect of different probiotic strains on sleep
1277	                           metrics including sleep latency.
1278	                                 Although evidence examining the effect of dietary supplementation on sleep was lim-
1279	                           ited, some dietary supplements appeared to be sleep promoting and, thus, warrant further
1280	                           investigation. The effect of cherry juice on athlete sleep had equivocal findings [70,71], with
1281	                           14% of rugby players surveyed perceiving non-specified sleep benefits following cherry
1282	                           juice supplementation [71]. Cherry juice provides an exogenous dietary source of mela-
1283	                           tonin, which has previously benefited the sleep of individuals with or without insomnia
1284	                           in the general population [106,107]. Further, supplementation of 100 mL beetroot juice
1285	                           improved markers of subjective sleep quality in one study of male athletes [74]. The most
1286	                           plausible mechanism of action is that the dietary nitrates contained within beetroot juice
1287	                           increase nitric oxide, a biological messenger involved in the modulation of sleep/wake
1288	                           states [108]. However, this study lacked detail on the population group, methodology, and
1289	                           overall findings, which casts doubt on the repeatability of the findings. With the popularity
1290	                           of beetroot juice use as an ergogenic aid increasing among athletes [109], further high-
1291	                           quality research is necessary to determine the relationship with sleep. Lastly, cannabidiol,
1292	                           a substance no longer prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency [110], may promote
1293	                           sleep. In one cohort of rugby players, 41% that had trialled CBD subjectively reported sleep
1294	                           improvements [77]. Although, a wide variety of supplemented CBD doses were reported
1295	                           (400 to 3000 mg), limiting the conclusions that can be drawn between the CBD–sleep re-
1296	                           lationship in athletic populations. In a large clinical population, 92% of patients that had
1297	                           trialled CBD found it helpful for their sleep [111]. Though CBD supplementation has seen
1298	                           improvements to the sleep of athletes and non-athletes, these studies have relied upon
1299	                           subjective measures of sleep.
1300	
1301	                           5. Limitations
1302	                                Though most studies included in this systematic review were regarded as of neutral
1303	                           or positive quality, many studies provided limited information on dietary controls and
1304	                           withdrawal/attrition rates within their studies. Many studies also did not implement
1305	                           validated subjective sleep tools to determine sleep outcomes, limiting the reliability of
1306	                           results across articles. Less than two-thirds of studies included in this review were RCTs
1307	                           (61%), limiting the ability to determine causality between sleep and certain dietary factors.
1308	                           Females were underrepresented within the literature, with only 20% of participants within
1309	                           the included RCTs being female. As the inclusion of studies within this review relied

1322	                                  Practical Applications
1323	                                  1.    Caffeine consumption (>2 mg·kg−1 body mass) prior to evening competition impairs
1324	                                        total sleep time, sleep latency, sleep efficiency, and wake after sleep onset.
1325	                                  2.    Evening consumption of protein sources high in tryptophan may help promote and
1326	                                        maintain the sleep of athletic populations, especially during times of typically dis-
1327	                                        turbed sleep (i.e., after competition).
1328	                                  3.    Consumption of high GI carbohydrates immediately after evening exercise may pro-
1329	                                        mote sleep.
1330	
1331	                                  6. Conclusions
1332	                                        This review supports the assertion that an athlete’s diet can impact their sleep. Dietary
1333	                                  factors may act as a practical tool to promote or inhibit the sleep of athletically trained pop-
1334	                                  ulations. Multiple sleep promoting factors were reviewed, including protein sources high
1335	                                  in tryptophan, high GI carbohydrate consumption in the evening, and sustained probiotic
1336	                                  supplementation. Caffeine was a sleep-inhibiting agent that appeared to negatively affect
1337	                                  athlete sleep several hours after consumption. There were few dietary supplements that
1338	                                  may promote sleep such as cherry juice and beetroot juice but require further investiga-
1339	                                  tion. With the evidence-base displaying that the sleep of athletically trained populations is
1340	                                  significantly influenced by diet, practitioners and athletes should strategically manipulate
1341	                                  macronutrient timing, type, dietary supplementation, and caffeine intake to optimize sleep
1342	                                  and performance outcomes.
